meta.title: Hindi B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Hindi → English (see the Hindi, recall the meaning) and English → Hindi (see an English meaning, recall the Hindi). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in their field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue, giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Hindi, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 152 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — politics and public administration, the law and the courts, the economy and finance, science and research, technology, the environment and natural resources, health and the mind, the arts, literature and the media, history and society, argument and evaluation — the words for claims, evidence, causes and consequences — the formal connectors of written Hindi, and the verbs of reporting, analysing and persuading — and the other 1348 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Hindi, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword is printed in Devanagari with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū for the long vowels, a tilde or a dot for nasalisation: khānā, ma͠i), so the deck can be studied before the script is fluent; the Hindi Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. The 952 nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, which every adjective, postposition and past-tense verb agrees with, and their plural; the 140 verbs show their past forms, where Hindi verbs are irregular, and behind the All forms fold their present, future, subjunctive and imperative by person. Real example sentences come with 520 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 151 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
